claims.text: AFI 16-701 (18 February 2014, 48 pages) identifies SAF/AAZ as 'the Secretary of the Air Force, Security, Counterintelligence, and Special Program Oversight' and requires all supplements to the instruction to be routed to SAF/AAZ for coordination before certification and approval.

Para. 2.1 assigns the Director, Security and Special Program Oversight (SAF/AAZ) to serve as principal advisor to SAF/AA for SAPs and as Director, AF SAPCO, developing SAP policy and directing, administering and overseeing the SAP security programme.

Para. 2.1.2.4 directs SAF/AAZ to 'establish a declassification program and ensure that necessary resources are applied to the review of information to ensure it is neither classified for longer than necessary nor declassified prematurely in accordance with the file series exemption'.

SAF/AAZ serves as Designated Accreditation Authority for all SAP information systems and as access approval authority for all SAPs, approving waivers for SAP access; both authorities may be delegated only in writing and must be revalidated annually.
The 2014 edition of AFI 16-701 was certified by SAF/AAZ, then Mr. Daniel F. McMillin, with SAF/AAZE as office of primary responsibility.

Placing SAP access approval and SAP declassification authority in the same office means the decision to disclose a programme is made by the official whose institutional interest is in the programme's continued protection. Reasoning: directly from the two responsibilities assigned in AFI 16-701 paras. 2.1.2.4 and 2.1.2.7.
Referenced by the board but no dossier written yet. This node exists so the graph resolves and so the gap is visible rather than silent — see the wave-3 queue.

connections.note: SAF/AAZ is the Air Force Special Access Program Central Office. Under AFPD 16-7 it administers Air Force SAPs on behalf of the Secretary of the Air Force while release of SAP material outside the department requires DoD SAPCO approval, placing SAF/AAZ inside the OSD-level special access architecture.

connections.edgeLabel: Air Force SAP directive bars congressional briefings without SAPCO approval
connections.label: United States House of Representatives
connections.note: Air Force Policy Directive 16-7, 'Special Access Programs,' 29 December 2010, states: 'It is strictly forbidden for any employee of the Air Force or any appropriately accessed organization or company to brief or provide SAP material to any Congressional Member or staff without DoD SAPCO approval. Additionally, the Director, SAF/AAZ will be kept informed of any interaction with Congress.' This is the documented mechanism behind the recurring complaint that SAP-compartmented material cannot reach non-HASC/HAC-D members.

desc: SAF/AAZ is the Secretary of the Air Force's Director of Security, Counterintelligence and Special Program Oversight, an office of the Air Force Secretariat sitting under the Administrative Assistant to the Secretary (SAF/AA). Air Force Instruction 16-701, 'Management, Administration and Oversight of Special Access Programs' (18 February 2014, OPR SAF/AAZE, certified by SAF/AAZ), assigns it the controlling role over every Air Force special access programme: SAF/AAZ is principal advisor to SAF/AA for SAPs, serves as Director of the Air Force SAP Central Office (AF SAPCO), develops SAP policy, directs and oversees the SAP security programme, serves as Designated Accreditation Authority for all SAP information systems, and serves as the access approval authority for all SAPs with power to approve waivers for SAP access. The same instruction directs SAF/AAZ to 'establish a declassification program' and to ensure information is neither classified longer than necessary nor declassified prematurely - meaning that the office that grants access to Air Force black programmes is also the office that decides when their contents may be released. That concentration is why this node matters. Any Air Force-hosted programme of the kind alleged on this board would be waived or unacknowledged under SAF/AAZ's oversight, its read-on list would be approved there, and any declassification would have to pass the same desk; it is simultaneously the gatekeeper of the secret and the arbiter of its disclosure, which is the structural conflict at the centre of the whole concealment argument.
